clarification_questions: Does the lead vocal have this problem solo, in context, or only on certain notes/moments?

Stacking several cuts before evaluating one.

rationale: The word “muddy” describes a perception, not a proven frequency or cause. For this lead vocal, plausible explanations include source tone, processing, relative level, masking, and monitoring.

recommended_first_experiment.action: First compare the source soloed and in context; if the mud exists in solo, test a small broad low-mid cut, otherwise test the competing source.
recommended_first_experiment.summary: First compare the source soloed and in context; if the mud exists in solo, test a small broad low-mid cut, otherwise test the competing source.
recommended_first_experiment.why_this_first: It is intended to distinguish likely causes before adding more processing or making a permanent move.

starting_points: Use low-mid search area only as a search orientation, not a preset.
For body, inspect roughly 120–350 Hz; for definition, inspect roughly 1–5 kHz; context decides whether either needs change.
stop_rule: Back off as soon as the named problem improves but the intended body, attack, clarity, or emotion begins to weaken.
teaching_principle: A tone word is a clue; use one reversible, context-aware test to identify the relationship causing it.
title: Diagnosing a muddy lead vocal
tradeoffs_and_risks: Too much cutting makes the source hollow or weak.
A louder or visually smoother curve may create false confidence.
undo_or_reset: Bypass/delete the diagnostic band and restore the saved plug-in output level.
what_to_listen_for: Clarity should improve while body and warmth remain.
Check whether guitars, keys become clearer or weaker when the target changes.
